title: New advanced material developed by incorporating metallic nanowires into MOFs can harness sunlight to degrade pollutants
body_text: A novel material developed by scientists through incorporating metallic nanowires into metal–organic framework (MOF), can harness a broad range of light wavelengths to efficiently degrade environmental pollutants like pyrene, a persistent polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH). Pyrene is a persistent pollutant and cause serious environmental problems because it is toxic to organisms and difficult to remediate. Scientists have been exploring ways of remediating Pyrene using Metal organic Frameworks (MOF), molecular constructions with large spaces through which gases and other chemicals can flow, the importance of which was recognized through the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2026. One-dimensional metallic nanowires are promising materials for capturing and using light because they can conduct electricity efficiently and interact strongly with light. Their unique structure helps them absorb more light. These properties make them attractive for developing advanced light-driven technologies. In particular, plasmonic photocatalysis offers a promising approach for sustainable energy and environmental applications because it can effectively utilize both visible and near-infrared light. Thus, incorporating metallic nanowires into MOFs can synergistically integrate the properties of both components. Researchers from the Institute of Advanced Study in Science and Technology (IASST), Guwahati, an Autonomous Institute under the Department of Science & Technology (DST), Govt. of India have developed an isoreticular (having the same underlying network topology as) metal–organic framework-8 (IRMOF-8)-confined copper nanowire (Cu NW)-based hybrid material that incorporates palladium (Pd) nanostructures to enhance light absorption and photocatalytic activity. At the same time, aluminum (Al) was chosen as an alternative to Pd because of its abundance, cost-effectiveness, and energetic plasmonic properties. The porous IRMOF-8 framework provides a confined environment for the nanowires, enabling close interactions among the components and facilitating efficient charge transfer. The incorporation of Pd significantly enhanced broadband light absorption via plasmonic interactions, while the earth-abundant Al-based system formed a promising antenna-reactor platform, thereby promoting interfacial charge transfer and photocatalytic disintegration of polybenzenoid hydrocarbon pollutants. The optimized integration of Pd into the copper nanowire (Cu NW) in metal–organic framework-8 (IRMOF-8) achieved 99% and Al into copper nanowire (Cu NW) in metal–organic framework-8 (IRMOF-8) achieved 85% removal of pyrene under the investigated irradiation and ultrasonication conditions. Fig: Schematic representation of the photocatalytic materials designed to target the disintegration of pyrene using solar energy combined with ultrasonication frequencies. The findings of this study led by Prof. Devasish Chowdhury, together with his PhD scholar Ms. Netra Prova Baruah, in collaboration with Prof. Mojibur R. Khan, Ms. Mandira Thakur, Ms. Ipsah Akhtar, Mr. Rahul Sonkar, and Prof. Arundhuti Devi recently published in ACS Applied Energy Materials, present a notable strategy for designing MOF-confined plasmonic nanomaterials for solar-harvesting photocatalysis and environmental remediation, especially in aquatic ecosystems. “The research is also an effort to develop aluminum (Al) -based system, which exhibited substantial photocatalytic performance, accentuating its potential to reduce reliance on noble metals,” said Prof. Chowdhury.
